meta.name: Claims over time: improving an appeals agent batch by batch
meta.question: When a claims-review agent meets new cases in batches, with only a few outcomes coming back each time, does an improver that works through recorded sessions and replays (the ZenML AI engineer with Kitaru) keep it improving better than a strong coding agent (Codex)?

dataset.source: California Independent Medical Review determinations, CalHHS Open Data

codex.change: Sparse residential-treatment summaries count as missing, not as evidence against

pro.change: The same idea for residential addiction treatment (ASAM levels 3.1 and 3.5)

codex.change: Don't infer necessity from a numeric score or an incidental finding alone

pro.change: Widen the residential rule to all residential appeals

codex.change: Tested widening its residential rule to other treatments

pro.change: Treat omissions as unknown in every review type
Output limit 4,096 to 8,192 tokens; request limit 12 to 16

codex.change: At most three precedent searches per appeal
Tested a rule on patient-specific criteria

pro.change: Autism therapy (ABA): dose and setting need patient-specific support

codex.change: Limit the missing-summary rule to residential appeals

pro.change: Named organs at risk count as evidence for proton beam

limitations: One state's medical-necessity and experimental-treatment reviews: written decisions, not insurers' claim files.
Case files are written by a model from decision texts that include the reviewer's reasoning. A check drops files with outcome wording, but the choice of facts can still hint at the outcome.
The comparison is uneven on purpose: Codex as a team without our know-how would run it, our AI engineer as the ZenML team runs it. It does not say how Codex would do with an expert's instructions.
Each design ran once. The first run, before we fixed what it exposed, found no difference between the three lines; a third run could rank them differently again.
The intervals cover which appeals were drawn, not how differently an improver might act on another night.
Balanced accuracy weighs a wrongful denial and a wrongful approval equally. An insurer, or a patient refused care, would not.
